Dr. Alvarez: Hi Mr. Thompson, hi Max. Thanks for coming in for the dental pre-op consult. Tell me what you've been seeing at home.
Owner: Max is nine, a Cavalier King Charles spaniel. His breath has been terrible for months, and lately he drops food while he chews and paws at his mouth. He still eats, but he's slower than before. Our last vet said he had dental disease two years ago and we kept putting it off.
Dr. Alvarez: That's understandable. Any sneezing, nasal discharge, bleeding from the mouth, or weight loss?
Owner: A little bleeding on his chew toy last week. No sneezing. His weight is stable I think. His energy is good, he's drinking normally. No vomiting.
Dr. Alvarez: Any other health problems or medications? I know Cavaliers often have heart trouble.
Owner: He has a heart murmur that was found three years ago. He takes pimobendan, one and a quarter milligrams, twice a day, that's what the cardiologist prescribed. No other medicines. He fasted this morning as instructed.
Dr. Alvarez: Good, thank you. In the consult room today he weighs 9.6 kilograms. Temperature 101.4 Fahrenheit, heart rate 110 beats per minute, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute. Body condition 5 out of 9. Mucous membranes pink, capillary refill under two seconds. I hear a grade three out of six left apical systolic murmur, which is consistent with his history. Lungs are clear.
Dr. Alvarez: Awake oral exam shows heavy calculus on all the cheek teeth, grade three gingivitis, and recession around the upper fourth premolars. A couple of the lower incisors are loose. The lower left first molar looks fractured and the gum is swollen.
Owner: What does that mean for the procedure?
Dr. Alvarez: We will do a full dental cleaning under general anesthesia, called a COHAT, with dental X-rays of the whole mouth, charting every tooth, and then treat what we find. I expect extractions, probably the loose incisors and the fractured molar, but we'll only know after the radiographs. Because of his heart, I want pre-anesthetic bloodwork and an updated chest X-ray first, and I'd like to speak with his cardiologist about the anesthetic plan. He'll be an ASA three patient.
Owner: How risky is it?
Dr. Alvarez: Any anesthetic carries some risk, and a heart condition raises it, but untreated dental infection also affects his heart and kidneys over time. We'll monitor him closely with ECG, blood pressure and oxygen levels, give nerve blocks for pain, and place an IV catheter with fluids. The estimate is on this sheet, with a range depending on the number of extractions.
Owner: Okay, I'd like to go ahead. Can we book for next Tuesday?
Dr. Alvarez: Yes. Fasting from midnight, but give his pimobendan with a small bite of food. Bring him at eight. After the procedure he'll need soft food for ten days and pain medication at home. I'll call you once he's awake.
